author: DANA ABBRING AND JOHN MILES Columnists
title: OPINION: The 2026 food pyramid scheme - NewsBreak
text:
By DANA ABBRING AND JOHN MILES Columnists ,
10 hours ago When the new dietary guidelines and the new food pyramid were released early last month, we were … confused.
This new food pyramid, or rather an upside-down food triangle, fails to serve as a solid nutrition guideline. There are a bunch of healthy foods featured like fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein, but also some questionable items like butter, fatty dairy, and red meat. How much of each should you be eating? Should everyone be eating the things pictured?
With all of these questions, we had to find answers. So, we sat down with Lauren Link, a registered dietitian and board certified specialist in sports dietetics, and an assistant athletic director of sports nutrition at Purdue.
“It reminds me of the original pyramid. I mean sure, we get the general gist. Eat more of these foods and less of these foods, but I don’t know how much to put on my plate,” Link said. “That’s why we went to MyPlate, which I think most dietitians and health professionals would agree is much more user-friendly.”
The first food pyramid was introduced in 1992. It replaced the "food wheel" and emphasized moderation and variety. Photo Courtesy of USDA The original pyramid refers to the Healthy Eating Period published in 1992, which was part of the first government-approved dietary guidelines for Americans. MyPlate was introduced in June 2011, and was an actual plate divided into sections to show how much of each food category someone should eat, replacing the food pyramid with something much easier to understand and implement.
MyPlate was introduced in 2011 alongside new USDA nutrition guidelines for Americans. It was further updated in 2020 with new research and a more streamlined design. Photo Courtesy of MyPlate.gov One interesting aspect of the new guidelines is that, unlike the pyramid diagram, they haven't changed all that much compared to guidelines laid out in the past.
“I think people have lost sight of that because nobody is really reading through the many pages that it is, they’re just seeing (the new pyramid)," Link said.
“The protein recommendation went up a little, which I’m like, 'cool, whatever.' The saturated fat recommendation didn’t change, which is good because we know saturated fat is bad for cardiovascular health. There’s no new science to refute that,” Link said.
While she recognized that many of these recommendations haven’t changed in the guidelines themselves, she pointed out how the new pyramid has plenty of items in the top left that are high in saturated fat, and seem to present a different picture than the guidelines do.
“If you’re a consumer who has very little nutrition knowledge, it would be hard, probably impossible, to meet the saturated fat recommendation by following this hierarchy,” Link said. “If I include even a couple of these foods, even just a serving a day, then I’m over (the recommendation).”
But beyond the new pyramid’s impracticality, there are problems with the items that make it up themselves. For example, the new pyramid has a whole stick of butter right in the middle of healthier foods like avocado, beans, and fruits. It’s like an imposter trying to just sneak by.
“Yeah, that’s an interesting choice, huh? I probably wouldn’t put a stick of butter next to grapes in terms of how fruit should function in our diet. It's a perfect example of it being misleading and confusing,” Link said. “Are you telling me that I should eat as much butter as I eat fruit?”
We also noticed the carton of whole milk, which has become a source of controversy for some.
“The only difference in whole milk is that it has a higher fat content, largely saturated fat, but it’s not so significant that I would be worried about it,” she said. “But it is kind of ironic because it’s contributing to saturated fat intake for a lot of Americans, and many people are trying to lose weight and improve cardiovascular health, which this doesn’t help.”
One problem that people had with old dietary guidelines was the concern that big industries like dairy and meat might have too big of an influence on the guidelines. This is part of the reason why some people were calling for a new set of guidelines.
However, the new guidelines and especially the new pyramid, the influence of these big industries is as strong as ever.
We asked Link how much dietitians rely on the dietary guidelines, and about the role that they play in nutrition education practice.
“With MyPlate, a dietitian might’ve downloaded it or other resources and used those with patients and clients, so it does guide some things,” she said. “We do use recommendations that come from the dietary guidelines, so the hope would be that they’re backed in science and that they’re always getting updated.”
Growing up with MyPlate, we remember just how simple and intuitive it was. To think that kids nowadays might have to grow up with the upside-down triangle instead just seems wrong. How will they really know what to eat?
Another part of the new guidelines that caught our attention was the removal of the daily alcohol limit, which was previously 2 drinks per day for men and 1 for women.
“It’s ironic, right? Alcohol is a known carcinogen, and with all of these people who are constantly shouting about toxins, they don’t seem as worried about alcohol,” Link said. “I don’t think it’s good for public health overall. I think it downplays the severity of it.”
Link also mentioned the harm that fearmongering has in nutrition, and we discussed how difficult it is for people to know who to trust online.
“Always follow the money. Working with athletes, my salary does not change regardless of what supplement you take or advice you follow,” she said. “But the person online who has an affiliate code absolutely has financial incentive.”
Additionally, people are often looking for quick fixes. It is something that grifters use to their advantage when they sell people their supplements. In reality, good health takes consistency, and we know what many of the fixes are, even if they’re not easy.
We asked her what she would change about the pyramid.
“I think that they’ve really downplayed beans and lentils which are crazy healthy but they’re not pictured here by themselves,” Link said. “They’re just in that bowl of rice.”
One thing that we do like about the new food pyramid is that it shows canned and frozen vegetables, which shows people that starting to eat healthier doesn’t necessarily have to be expensive. It’s better for people to eat any vegetables than none at all, and Link agreed.
Finally, we asked, if she could redo the pyramid herself, what would she do?
“I’d turn it into a plate,” she replied. “And I would divide that plate into what each meal should look like.”
And we agree.
